prompt: Where does the lesson get the growth rate of `orders` from?
hint: The database already contains its own history.

choices.text: From counting orders by month of `placed_at`
choices.why: Right: every dated row records when it arrived.

choices.text: From the size of the table in yesterday's backup
choices.why: One backup is one snapshot; growth needs a history, which the rows already carry.

choices.text: From a forecast written by the business
choices.why: The lesson measures rather than asks.

choices.text: From `pg_stat_statements`
choices.why: It counts statements since a reset, not rows over three years.

prompt: The monthly counts go up by roughly the same two to three thousand orders each month. What kind of growth is that, and why does it matter?
hint: A fixed amount against a fixed percentage.

choices.text: Exponential, so the disk fills in months
choices.why: Exponential would curve upwards; these steps are about the same size.

choices.text: Seasonal, so it cannot be forecast
choices.why: February's dip is the short month; the trend underneath is plain.

choices.text: Linear: a straight-line forecast works
choices.why: Right: a shop growing by a percentage would need the curve instead.

choices.text: None: the counts are random
choices.why: They rise steadily month after month.

prompt: Why is 130 bytes per order more than the five columns of an order would suggest?
hint: What was divided by what?

choices.text: PostgreSQL stores numbers as text
choices.why: Integers and timestamps are stored in fixed binary widths.

choices.text: It counts indexes, row overhead and free space
choices.why: Right: pg_total_relation_size divided by the rows includes all of that.

choices.text: Because the estimate of rows is too low
choices.why: reltuples for orders was exactly 2000000.

choices.text: Because deleted orders still take space
choices.why: Nothing was deleted from orders.

prompt: A forecast of the disk is made from `orders` and `order_lines` alone. By roughly how much is it wrong on this database?
hint: Which table grows fastest in bytes?

choices.text: Not at all: events are not part of the database's size
choices.why: events is the largest table of all.

choices.text: By about 10%
choices.why: events add 217 MB a month against 39 for the other two.

choices.text: By a factor of about six, because events grow more than everything else
choices.why: Right: 256 MB a month in total against 39 for orders and lines.

choices.text: By a factor of a hundred
choices.why: The ratio is about 256 to 39.

prompt: A disk has 20 GB free and the database grows by 256 MB a month. Roughly how many months until it is full? (1 GB = 1024 MB)
hint: Free space divided by growth.

prompt: Which of these take disk space that a forecast built from row counts does not see? Choose all that apply.
hint: The last paragraph of the growth section.

choices.text: The write-ahead log
choices.why: Right: it grows with the writes, not as rows.

choices.text: Temporary files from a large sort
choices.why: Right: they appear while a query runs.

choices.text: A backup written to the same disk
choices.why: Right: it grows with the database without being in it.

choices.text: The rows of `orders`
choices.why: Those are exactly what the forecast counts.

prompt: What does `pgbench -R 600` change about how the workload is sent?
hint: Real users do not wait for the server to be ready.

choices.text: It sends 600 transactions and stops
choices.why: That would be a transaction count; -R is a rate.

choices.text: It sets a pace, as users arrive, and counts the wait
choices.why: Right: when the server falls behind, the schedule lag is part of the latency.

choices.text: It caps each transaction at 600 ms
choices.why: Nothing is cut off; the rate is what is fixed.

choices.text: It runs 600 clients
choices.why: Clients are -c; the run used eight.

prompt: At 1050 transactions a second the server delivered `tps = 1042` with an average latency of 133 ms. What happened?
hint: It did not fail.

choices.text: It kept up by making everybody queue
choices.why: Right: the rate was met, and the price was waiting.

choices.text: It dropped the transactions it could not handle
choices.why: No transaction failed; they waited.

choices.text: The disk filled during the run
choices.why: Nothing in the run points at the disk; the latency grew with the rate.

choices.text: pgbench mismeasured, because 1050 is above the maximum
choices.why: 1050 is below the measured maximum of 1099.

prompt: The server's maximum is 1100 transactions a second. Your manager asks to run it at 1000, "since we still have 10% headroom". What does the lesson's measurement say about that?
hint: Read the percentiles, not the average.

choices.text: It is fine: 10% is the usual safety margin
choices.why: At 1000 the slowest users already waited over half a second.

choices.text: Past the knee: p99 was 621 ms
choices.why: Right: headroom is distance from the knee, not from the maximum.

choices.text: It will fail with errors above 1000
choices.why: It did not fail at 1050; it queued.

choices.text: The average of 62 ms is acceptable, so yes
choices.why: 62 ms was the median; the tail is what users complain about.

prompt: In the rated runs, what was the average latency, in milliseconds, at 900 transactions a second? Round to the nearest whole number.
hint: The third rated run.

prompt: The point on the curve where the latency stops growing slowly and starts growing fast is called the ___.
hint: A joint of the leg.

prompt: At 600 a second the median transaction took 0.7 ms and the 99th percentile 93.5 ms. What does the gap say?
hint: The queue does not delay everybody equally.

choices.text: The log file was corrupted during the run
choices.why: The numbers are consistent with a mix of cheap and expensive queries.

choices.text: Half the workload failed
choices.why: No transaction failed in these runs.

choices.text: A few wait behind slow ones
choices.why: Right: the average hides the people who waited.

choices.text: The server is out of disk
choices.why: Disk space has nothing to do with this spread.

prompt: What happens to a client that asks for a connection when `max_connections` are already in use?
hint: Refused or queued?

choices.text: It waits until one is free
choices.why: The server keeps no queue for connections.

choices.text: It is refused with an error
choices.why: Right: lesson 16 shows the error and what to do instead.

choices.text: The oldest connection is closed to make room
choices.why: Nothing is closed to make room.

choices.text: The server raises the limit automatically
choices.why: max_connections is fixed at start-up.

prompt: A table with a few thousand rows has an `integer` key whose sequence is near 2147483647. How is that possible?
hint: Does a sequence give numbers back?

choices.text: The sequence counts bytes, not rows
choices.why: It hands out one number per call.

choices.text: Somebody set the sequence by hand to a high value
choices.why: Possible, but the lesson names a reason that needs nobody's mistake.

choices.text: Deletes and rollbacks spent numbers too
choices.why: Right: a sequence never gives a number back.

choices.text: `integer` sequences count by two
choices.why: They count by one unless told otherwise.

prompt: Why does the lesson call the transaction counter "the wall that almost never arrives"?
hint: Who is built to prevent it?

choices.text: Autovacuum freezes rows before it wraps
choices.why: Right: it arrives only when something stops VACUUM from freezing.

choices.text: Because the counter is 64 bits
choices.why: It is 32 bits, which is why it wraps after about four billion.

choices.text: Because a restart of the server resets it to zero
choices.why: A restart changes nothing about transaction ids.

choices.text: Because only replicas have one
choices.why: Every server has it.

prompt: Match each wall to how it shows up when it is reached.
hint: Some refuse, some fail one statement.

pairs.right: the INSERT that crossed it fails
new transactions are refused until a vacuum catches up

prompt: Why does the lesson suggest alerting on an `integer` sequence a year before it runs out?
hint: How long does the fix take?

choices.text: Sequences slow down gradually as they get close to the limit
choices.why: They do not; they stop.

choices.text: The fix rewrites the table; it needs planning and a window
choices.why: Right: the alert must leave time for a calm migration.

choices.text: Because the law requires a year's notice
choices.why: No law is involved.

choices.text: Because autovacuum resets sequences once a year
choices.why: Autovacuum never touches sequences.

prompt: What does the lesson say an alert should measure, instead of a percentage?
hint: A distance divided by a speed.

choices.text: The time left before the wall
choices.why: Right: how far from the limit, divided by how fast it is approaching.

choices.text: The absolute size of the database in gigabytes
choices.why: A size says nothing about when it will matter.

choices.text: The number of alerts already sent today
choices.why: That measures the alerting, not the database.

choices.text: The average query time across the whole application
choices.why: An average hides the slow tail and says nothing about walls.

prompt: Put the steps of turning `capacity.sql` into an alert in order.
hint: A snapshot, then a trend, then a threshold.
items: Keep each run's rows somewhere else
Compute each wall's growth per day from two runs
Divide what is left by that growth
Fire when the time left is under the fix's duration plus a margin
trap: A trend needs two kept snapshots; the threshold comes last because it depends on the time left.

prompt: A disk has 90 GB left and grows by 3 GB a day. Ordering and attaching a bigger disk takes two weeks. How many days of margin are left beyond the fix's two weeks?
hint: Time left minus the fix.

prompt: A query took 10 ms yesterday and 40 ms today; nothing is near any wall. Should it raise an alert?
hint: Level against change.

choices.text: No: 40 ms is fast
choices.why: The level is fine; the change is the signal.

choices.text: No: alerts are only for walls
choices.why: The lesson names two alerts that are not about walls.

choices.text: Yes: a fourfold change is the first sign of stale statistics or a plan outgrown
choices.why: Right: alert on change as well as level.

choices.text: Yes, but only if the disk is above 80%
choices.why: The disk has nothing to do with this query's change.

prompt: The database holds 400 GB on a 1 TB disk and grows by 5 GB a week; a second server's disk is 70% full after five years of slow growth. Which needs attention first?
hint: Time left, not percentage.

choices.text: The second: 70% is higher than 40%
choices.why: Five years to reach 70% leaves years more.

choices.text: Neither: both are under 80%
choices.why: A percentage threshold is the alert the lesson argues against.

choices.text: The first: about 120 weeks left
choices.why: Right: 600 GB at 5 GB a week is about 120 weeks; still calm, but the nearer of the two.

choices.text: Both equally, because both will fill
choices.why: Equal urgency ignores the rates.
